summary.text: Mass-energy equivalence says an object's energy in its rest frame equals its mass multiplied by the speed of light squared, written E = mc².
Because light's speed is huge and gets squared, a small amount of mass corresponds to an enormous amount of energy.
When mass is lost in chemical or nuclear reactions, a matching amount of energy is released as radiant energy such as light, or as thermal energy.

facts.label: One kilogram
facts.value: Corresponds to about 10¹⁷ joules of energy

facts.label: Rest mass
facts.value: The same in all inertial frames

facts.label: Photons
facts.value: Zero invariant mass, yet they carry energy

items.prompt: In a nuclear reactor, the atoms that come out weigh slightly less than the atoms that went in. Where did the missing mass go?

options.label: It vanished with no trace at all
It became extra atoms outside the reactor
It became heat and light of equivalent energy
It stayed inside as hidden mass in the walls

items.explain: The difference in mass shows up as heat and light carrying the equivalent energy.

items.prompt: A perfectly mirrored sealed box is filled with trapped light. Does the box weigh more than the same empty box?

options.label: No, since photons have no mass at all
Yes, by the light's energy divided by c²
No, but it would feel hotter
Yes, by the number of photons times their mass

items.explain: Individually massless photons still add to the box's total mass by an amount equal to their energy divided by c².

items.prompt: A particle zooms past you in a lab, and a friend riding along with it measures its rest mass too. How do the two rest-mass values compare?

options.label: Yours is bigger because of its motion
Your friend's is bigger since they ride along
They match, since rest mass does not depend on the observer's motion
They differ by the particle's kinetic energy

items.explain: Rest mass is the same for all inertial frames, because it is independent of the motion of the observer.

items.prompt: Why does losing even a tiny amount of mass correspond to such a vast release of energy?

options.label: Matter is made mostly of stored fuel
The conversion factor is a large number multiplied by itself
Mass is always lost faster than it gets measured
Energy is measured in very small units

items.explain: The factor is the speed of light squared, and since light is fast and the number is squared, a little mass equals a lot of energy.

items.prompt: A chemist insists that mass is conserved in every interaction without exception. What does special relativity say about this?

options.label: It agrees, since mass can never change at all
It says energy is the one thing that is not conserved
Mass is not conserved there, but energy is
It says momentum is the quantity that fails to hold

items.explain: Mass is not conserved in special relativity, whereas conservation of momentum and conservation of energy are both fundamental laws.

items.prompt: A rock sits perfectly still on a table. According to mass-energy equivalence, does it carry any energy?

options.label: No, since a motionless body has no energy
Yes, it has an intrinsic energy tied to its mass
Only if the table is warm
Only the energy of its position in a field

items.explain: All massive objects have a corresponding intrinsic energy, even when stationary.

paragraphs.heading: What the idea says
paragraphs.text: Mass–energy equivalence is the link between an object's mass and its energy, taken in the object's rest frame, the viewpoint in which it sits still. Einstein summed it up in the formula E = mc², where E is energy, m is mass and c is the speed of light. Mass and energy differ only by a constant multiplier and by the units used to measure them. So anything with mass carries its own built-in energy, even when it is not moving at all.

paragraphs.heading: Why a little mass goes a long way
paragraphs.text: The speed of light is a big number, and the formula squares it. That means a small amount of mass matches an enormous amount of energy. For one kilogram, mc² comes to something on the order of 10¹⁷ joules. The chemical or heat energy stored inside an ordinary resting object tends to be far smaller than that.

paragraphs.heading: Where the energy goes
paragraphs.text: When a chemical or nuclear reaction loses some mass, a matching amount of energy is let out. In a nuclear reaction, the atoms that come out have less mass than the atoms that went in. The missing mass turns up as heat and light carrying the equivalent energy. To work this out, E is read as the energy released and m as the change in mass.

paragraphs.heading: Adding and removing energy
paragraphs.text: The rule also runs the other way. All the energy that travels along with an object adds to its total mass, which measures how hard the object is to speed up. Imagine an isolated box of perfect mirrors that could hold light: the photons have no mass one by one, yet together they add their energy divided by c² to the box's mass. Taking energy out removes mass by m = E/c², and putting energy into an isolated system raises its mass by the same amount.

paragraphs.heading: Rest mass and moving mass
paragraphs.text: Physicists talk about two kinds of mass. Rest mass, also called invariant mass, is the mass an object has when it is not moving relative to the observer, and it does not depend on how the observer moves. Relativistic mass does change with motion: a moving object has more of it because it has kinetic energy, the energy of motion, so different observers get different values. Since relativistic mass is really just energy under another name, physicists usually keep the word mass for rest mass.

paragraphs.heading: A whole is not its parts added up
paragraphs.text: One surprise is that masses do not simply add. The parts of a system pull on each other, which gives them potential energy, and the rest mass of the whole counts all the energy of its parts, including their motion. So in general an object's mass is not the total of its pieces' masses. The plain sum only works when the parts are at rest and neither attract nor repel each other.

paragraphs.heading: Where it came from
paragraphs.text: In the late 1800s, people explored some connection between mass and energy under the name electromagnetic mass. The French polymath Henri Poincaré described it as a paradox arising from special relativity. Einstein was the first to put it forward as a general principle that follows from the symmetries of space and time. It appeared in his paper of 21 November 1905, and today it is basic to nuclear and particle physics.
